d: Scope the prompt, do the napkin math, design the two API calls, and choose 301 or 302
goal: Your win today: in the first five minutes you can ask the right scoping questions, work out about 1,160 writes/s, 11,600 reads/s, 365 billion records and 36.5 TB, name the two endpoints, and say when you'd use 301 vs 302.
bookSections: Step 1 (Understand the problem: requirements, back-of-the-envelope estimation); Step 2 (API endpoints, URL redirecting with 301 vs 302, URL shortening overview)

stages.title: Ask before you draw
stages.teaches: The book's prompt is 'design a URL shortener like TinyURL'. Example: https://www.systeminterview.com/q=chatsystem&c=loggedin&v=v3&l=long becomes https://tinyurl.com/y7keocwj, and clicking the short alias redirects to the original. Answers from the book's dialogue: traffic is 100 million URLs generated per day; the short URL should be as short as possible; allowed characters are 0-9, a-z and A-Z; for simplicity, short URLs can't be deleted or updated. Basic use cases: (1) shortening, long URL in, short URL out; (2) redirecting, short URL in, redirect to the long URL. Non-functional needs: high availability, scalability, fault tolerance.
stages.interaction: A 'question deck' of 9 cards. The learner taps the 5 they'd ask the interviewer first. Good cards: 'Can you give an example?', 'What is the traffic volume?', 'How short must the short URL be?', 'Which characters are allowed?', 'Can short URLs be deleted or updated?'. Distractor cards: 'Which programming language?', 'Should I use Kubernetes?', 'What colour is the logo?', 'Should we use MongoDB?'. When a good card is tapped it flips over and shows the interviewer's answer (from the book) in a speech bubble, and that answer is pinned to a 'Requirements' sticky note in the corner, where it stays for later stages. Tapping a distractor gives a gentle shake and a reason ('a tool choice, not a requirement; decide it later'). The stage is done when all 5 good cards are flipped.
stages.check: Q.quiz with 3 questions: (1) Which two use cases make up the core of the system? (shortening + redirecting); (2) What did the interviewer say about deletes/updates? (not allowed, a simplification); (3) Which characters may appear in the short code? (0-9, a-z, A-Z = 62).

stages.title: Napkin math
stages.sub: Back-of-the-envelope, then play with the knobs
stages.teaches: Write ops: 100 million/day ÷ 86,400 s ≈ 1,160 per second. Read:write is assumed to be 10:1, so reads ≈ 11,600 per second. Running for 10 years: 100M × 365 × 10 = 365 billion records. With an average URL length of 100 bytes, storage over 10 years = 365 billion × 100 B = 36.5 TB. Tip: round freely (a day ≈ 100k seconds) and say your assumptions out loud.
stages.interaction: Calculate-and-check: four input boxes (writes/s, reads/s, records in 10 years, storage in 10 years) with unit dropdowns (K/M/B/T and GB/TB). Each answer is accepted within ±10% (writes 1,045–1,275 etc.). Show a 'hint' button per box that reveals the formula. After all four are correct, the boxes turn into live outputs driven by four sliders: URLs/day (10M–1B), read:write ratio (1:1–100:1), years (1–20), average URL bytes (50–500). The learner is asked to answer a mini-challenge: 'Drag the sliders until storage passes 100 TB; which knob moved it fastest?', with no single answer, just reflection text.
stages.check: Stage clears when all four boxes are correct. Short Q.quiz (2 questions): 'If the read:write ratio were 100:1, reads/s ≈ ?' (≈116,000); 'Which number tells you how long the short code must be?' (365 billion records).

stages.title: Two doors in
stages.teaches: REST-style API, two endpoints. (1) URL shortening: POST api/v1/data/shorten, request body {longUrl: longURLString}, returns the shortURL. (2) URL redirecting: GET api/v1/shortUrl, returns the longURL for HTTP redirection. POST because it creates a new resource; GET because a redirect is a read that browsers perform automatically when someone clicks a link.
stages.interaction: Build-the-request: two empty request cards ('Shorten' and 'Redirect'). For each card the learner picks a method chip (GET / POST / PUT / DELETE), a path chip (api/v1/data/shorten, api/v1/{shortUrl}, api/v1/urls/all) and a body chip (none / {longUrl} / {shortUrl}). A 'Send' button fires the request into a mock server that answers with a response panel: correct combos return 200 + shortURL or a 301/302 + Location header; wrong combos return a playful 405/404 with an explanation. Done when both cards return a successful response.
stages.check: Q.quiz with 2 questions: why POST for shorten (creates a new mapping, not idempotent read); what the GET endpoint returns (the long URL inside an HTTP redirect, not a page).

stages.title: 301 or 302?
stages.teaches: When the server receives a short URL it answers with a redirect: a status code plus a Location header holding the long URL. 301 Moved Permanently: the browser caches the response, so later requests for the same short URL go straight to the long URL and never reach the shortener; good for cutting server load. 302 Found (temporarily moved): every request goes to the shortener first, then is redirected; good when analytics matter (click rate, where clicks come from). Interview line: 301 to save load, 302 to track clicks.
stages.interaction: Predict-then-watch simulation. On screen: a browser (left), the shortener server with a 'requests seen' counter and an 'analytics clicks' counter (middle), and the destination site (right). A toggle selects 301 or 302. Before running, the learner predicts: 'After 3 clicks of the same short link, how many requests will the shortener see?' (choices 0 / 1 / 3). Then they press 'Click link' three times; animated packets travel browser→shortener→browser→destination. With 301, click 1 goes via the shortener, then a 'cached 301' badge appears on the browser and clicks 2–3 jump straight to the destination (counter stays at 1). With 302, every click goes via the shortener (counter 3). The learner must run and predict both codes; a 'Clear browser cache' button resets the browser badge.
stages.check: Both predictions entered and both runs watched (wrong predictions cost no hearts but show the reason). Then Q.quiz with 2 questions: 'Marketing wants per-click stats on every click' → 302; 'Which header holds the long URL?' → Location.

stages.title: The obvious version
stages.sub: Step 2 · shortening with a hash table
stages.teaches: The simplest shortening idea: a hash table of <shortURL, longURL> pairs. A hash function fx(longURL) = hashValue, and the short URL is www.tinyurl.com/{hashValue}. Requirements on the function: each long URL must map to one hashValue, and each hashValue must map back to its long URL. This sets up the deep dive: where to store the table (365B rows won't fit in memory) and how to make fx produce short, unique values.
stages.interaction: Mini-sim: a small in-memory table that the learner fills by typing long URLs; each gets a fake 7-char code. A RAM gauge for the server fills based on the 10-year projection (36.5 TB vs a 256 GB server); when the learner clicks 'Fast-forward 10 years' the gauge overflows in red with the message 'In-memory hash table won't hold 365 billion rows; we need a database'. This is a cliff-hanger that hands off to quest 8.2.
stages.check: One Q.quiz question: 'Why can't the whole mapping live in a single server's memory hash table?' (36.5 TB+ over 10 years, far more than one machine's RAM; also lost on restart).

stages.title: Boss: The Redirect Riddler
stages.sub: Pick the right status code for each client
stages.teaches: Applying 301 vs 302 and the estimates to concrete client asks.
stages.interaction: Q.boss with choices [{k:'301', label:'301 Moved Permanently', sub:'browser caches it'}, {k:'302', label:'302 Found', sub:'every click hits us'}]. Scenarios (6): marketing team needs click-through rate per campaign → 302; a static docs site, servers are overloaded, nobody reads stats → 301; A/B test that may switch the destination next week → 302; mass printed QR codes on posters pointing to a page that will never move, minimise cost → 301; fraud team wants to see the referrer and country of every click → 302; a link checker crawls the same short URL thousands of times a day and you want to stop paying for it → 301. Each 'why' cites caching vs analytics.
stages.check: Boss cleared when all scenarios answered (engine handles hearts).

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.sub: The first five minutes, out loud
stages.teaches: Pulling scope, estimates, API and redirect choice into one answer.
stages.interaction: Q.drill. Prompt: interviewer says 'Design a URL shortener like TinyURL. Go.' Placeholder: 'Before I draw anything, I'd like to ask…'. Model answer: 'First I'd scope it: an example, the traffic (say 100M new URLs a day), how short the URL must be, which characters (0-9, a-z, A-Z) and whether links can be deleted (no). Then quick math: about 1,160 writes/s, 10:1 reads so about 11,600 reads/s, 365 billion records over 10 years, about 36.5 TB at 100 bytes each. Two endpoints: POST /api/v1/data/shorten with the long URL, and GET /api/v1/{shortUrl}, which redirects. I'd use 302 if we care about click analytics, 301 if we'd rather the browser cache it to save load.' Checks: ['I asked about traffic, length, characters and deletes before designing', 'I gave writes/s, reads/s, record count and storage', 'I named both endpoints and the 301-vs-302 trade-off'].

caveats: Real shorteners mostly use 301 (bit.ly and TinyURL send 301s) and still collect analytics, because browsers don't cache 301s forever and the first click per browser is logged. The book's '301 = no analytics' is a useful simplification, not a law.
There are also 307 and 308 (like 302 and 301, but the browser must keep the HTTP method). For GET-only redirects, 301 and 302 are fine; mention 307/308 only if asked.
36.5 TB counts only the long URLs. Real storage is higher: short codes, IDs, timestamps, indexes and replicas (×3) multiply it.
10:1 read:write is the book's assumption; popular shorteners are far more read-heavy, which strengthens the case for caching.
The API path GET api/v1/shortUrl is the book's notation; in practice the redirect lives at the root (https://tinyurl.com/{code}) so the short URL stays short.
